Thank you for submitting your article "On the objectivity, reliability, and validity of deep learning enabled bioimage analyses" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Marianne Bronner as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Dan Ruderman (Reviewer #1); Gaudenz Danuser (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission. We all feel that this manuscript will be ready for acceptance after some minor revisions, not requiring re-review.

I agree with all three reviewers that this manuscript is a significant step forward. Reviewer 3 summarized the manuscript and its strengths nicely: "This is a very high quality evaluation of procedures that should be put in place to set up objective, reliable, and valid Deep Learning models for fluorescence image segmentation. I commend the authors for teaming up multiple labs in order to build consensus “ground truth” models. They have done an impressive amount of work in documenting the performance of the various strategies for generating training data sets. The paper is written very well. Despite the dryness of the subject and the at times dense lines of argumentation, one can get through the material in a reasonable amount of time, and then go deep where necessary. This paper can become the reference for every investigator starting a quantitative imaging study with deep learning."

The reviewers and I would like to offer some suggested changes to the presentation, without requiring the addition of more experimental work or analyses:

1) Figures and Tables.

A) Both reviewer 2 and I found Figure 1 a bit confusing and I found at least three different ways that it could be misunderstood. The problem is that the workflow icons in the individual vertical boxes appear to lie up with the horizontal bars, which I do not believe is your intent. Please revise Figure 1 so that your intent is more clear. I suggest that changing the scale and spacing of the icons might solve it, but putting the workflow icons below the horizontal bars would make the figure only slightly larger and make your intent much more clear.

B) Please use similar scales and formats for figures that readers are likely to compare, and might misunderstand. For example Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4 are slightly different sizes, and use different scales (what the different shades of gray represent), so I found myself puzzled. Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 5—figure supplement 4 use different scales as well.

C) Table 1, and elsewhere in the text needs attention to the number of significant figures that are displayed. Table 1 shows p-values to 5 or 4 significant figures for non-significant differences. It shows p-values to 3 significant figures for some of the significant differences. If the authors reflect on this, I believe they will agree that there is no way that the data set is sufficiently large for this number of significant figures. Furthermore, the large number of figures distract the reader from the message I believe the authors are intending to convey.

2) Language and definitions.

A) The reviewers point out that this very strong paper is not made stronger by claims that seem beyond beyond the data. These include the claim that the DL approach surpasses the experts.

B) There are terms that should be clarified or defined; in most of these cases, it might be wise to find language that is less likely to be misunderstood. These include: "invalid", "bad", "biased", "irreproducible", "appear to alter the results", "DL models are proven to…" etc. Note that all of these should be easy to resolve, but could confuse, anger and/or frustrate a reader, which will not optimize the acceptance of the important lessons of this work.

Reviewer #1:

This work is high quality, employs real-world data sets from multiple sources, and addresses questions of broad interest. I recommend publication in eLife.

Reviewer #2:

In general, I really enjoyed reading this manuscript, and I think the new focus resulted in a much clearer paper compared with the previous version. As a researcher in machine learning myself, the manuscript includes several findings that I will use in my future research, especially the comparison between the various training approaches. As such, I think that the paper will be a valuable contribution to the field, and I recommend publication after my comments below (and those of other reviewers) have been addressed. Note that my expertise is in developing machine learning algorithms, and I don't have enough background in the specific biology application to feel comfortable with commenting on the validity of the biology.

1) My main concern with respect to the method is the exclusion of what the authors call “invalid” methods in the ensemble approaches. By construction, this exclusion biases the results towards better metrics. Therefore, it is not entirely clear whether the better performance of the ensemble approaches is caused by the ensemble itself, or rather simply by the fact that multiple networks were trained and “bad” networks were thrown away. This question can be answered in several ways: for example, it would already be informative to know how many networks were rejected in this way (if it is a small number compared with the total number of networks, it is not likely the improvement is due to the rejection). Even better would be to also apply the same rejection strategy to the expert model approach and see whether that improves these by the same amount (even though you would have access to the estimated GT in pure expert model applications).

2) My second main concern is with regards to practical application of the consensus ensemble approach. In many applications, it is very time consuming to acquire manually annotated images due to the required expertise for manual annotation and the time it takes to annotate. Therefore, getting enough manual annotations to obtain accurate consensus models might be prohibitively difficult in practice. A solution for this might be to use multiple experts, but have each expert annotate a different set of images. This would drastically reduce the required manual annotation time compared with obtaining a full consensus model, but you would still have information from multiple experts, which might improve results. For the current manuscript, it would be very informative to include this approach in the results. One way of doing this is to use the data that the authors already have, assign each of the 36 training images to one of the 5 experts, and then during training only use the manual annotation of the assigned expert for that image.

3) To me Figure 1 is quite hard to read. I do get what the authors mean, but the fact that the icons in the “vertical blocks” (e.g. “data annotation” and “automated annotation”) align with the rows makes it seem that each icon in the block actually belongs to a certain row. A solution would be to rearrange the icons inside each block somewhat (e.g. by making them smaller) so that they don't line up anymore with the rows.

4) It would be interesting to investigate what the accuracy is of an approach in which only the GT of a single expert is used, but multiple networks are trained in an ensemble. In other words, a combination between the expert models and consensus ensembles, but without using the estimated GT. This would indicate whether the improvement of the consensus ensembles is not purely due to the ensemble itself. I don't expect that this will actually achieve very accurate results, so probably a short paragraph or an added sentence or two will be enough to describe these additional results in the paper.

This paper can become the reference for every investigator starting a quantitative imaging study with deep learning. I really have nothing substantial to comment.

results.result: Manual annotation of fluorescent features with low signal-to-noise ratios is subjective and depends on individual annotator perception. This subjectivity poses challenges for training deep learning models, as there is no objective ground truth in fluorescent label segmentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C7-C9, C19-C20 establish the problem context through cited literature and general knowledge about fluorescence imaging. The claims are mutually consistent and well-supported by multiple citations (Schmitz et al., 1999; Collier et al., 2003; Niedworok et al., 2016; Cleveland and McGill, 1985), establishing the foundation for the study's motivation.

results.result: Deep learning approaches have emerged as alternatives to traditional image thresholding methods for bioimage analysis, offering flexibility to learn tasks from training data. However, deployment requires computational expertise and suitable resources, prompting efforts to integrate DL into accessible bioimaging tools.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C17 describe the state of the field regarding DL in bioimage analysis, supported by multiple citations (Li et al., 2010; McDole et al., 2018; Sezgin and Sankur, 2004; LeCun et al., 2015; Falk et al., 2019; McQuin et al., 2018). These are well-established facts in the field and provide appropriate background context.

results.result: DL-based approaches must meet standards of objectivity, reliability, and validity. While repeatability is guaranteed for deterministic models, reproducibility is challenged by stochastic training procedures. Standard DL practices do not apply when ground truth is absent, potentially aggravating the reproducibility crisis in biology and AI.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C22-C28 establish the quality criteria framework (supported by Frambach et al., 2013; Taylor and Kuyatt, 1994) and identify limitations of current DL practices. The claims about reproducibility crisis are supported by multiple citations (Siebert et al., 2015; Baker, 2016; Ioannidis, 2016; Hutson, 2018; Fanelli, 2018; Chen et al., 2019). The logical progression from established standards to identified gaps is sound.

results.result: The study employs U-Net architecture as the standard for biomedical image segmentation and uses STAPLE for ground truth estimation. Model ensembles are known to be robust to noise and provide high-quality uncertainty estimates. The cFOS label in mouse brain sections serves as an ideal test case due to its low signal-to-noise ratio and well-established behavioral correlations.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36 describe methodological choices supported by appropriate citations (McQuin et al., 2018; Falk et al., 2019; Caicedo et al., 2019; Warfield et al., 2004; Dietterich, 2000; Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017; Gallo et al., 2018; Shuvaev et al., 2017). The rationale for using cFOS as a test case is well-justified based on its properties and established use in neuroscience.

results.result: Analysis of manual annotations from five independent experts revealed substantial inter-rater variability that was inversely correlated with signal intensity. Expert models successfully learned and reproduced the annotation behavior of individual experts, including their biases.
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C39-C41 describe experimental findings supported by data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and citations (Schmitz et al., 1999; Collier et al., 2003; Niedworok et al., 2016; von Chamier et al., 2019). The inverse correlation between variability and signal intensity is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The conclusion that expert models reproduce individual biases is a reasonable inference from the similarity analysis data.

results.result: Consensus ensembles outperformed all other strategies in similarity metrics, achieving performance on par with human experts while showing substantially higher reliability (Fleiss' kappa indicating substantial to almost perfect agreement). Only the consensus ensemble strategy meets bioimaging standards for objectivity, reliability, and validity.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C49 present the core similarity analysis results supported by multiple figures (Figure 2F-H, Figure 2—figure supplement 3-4). The statistical analysis using Fleiss' kappa is appropriate and properly interpreted using Landis and Koch, 1977 criteria. The conclusion that consensus ensembles meet all three quality criteria is well-supported by the comprehensive similarity analysis data.

results.result: Bioimage analysis of cFOS in mouse hippocampus after contextual fear conditioning revealed context-dependent increases in cFOS abundance across most hippocampal regions. All three DL strategies showed identical majority votes at p≤0.05, but expert models trained on expert 1 annotations failed to detect significant increases in mean signal intensity, demonstrating bias incorporation.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 present biological validation results supported by extensive neuroscience literature (Keiser et al., 2017; Campeau et al., 1997; Huff et al., 2006; and others), behavioral data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and bioimage analysis results (Figure 4A-E). The finding that expert 1 models failed to detect effects demonstrates bias propagation. Statistical analyses are appropriate (Mann-Whitney-U tests with Bonferroni correction).

results.result: Consensus ensembles yielded significantly lower standard deviation of effect sizes compared to alternative strategies. Model-to-model variability was identified as the main factor impairing reproducibility, and no expert model detected all biological effects defined by majority votes. Consensus ensembles significantly reduce the risk of irreproducible results.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59, C80-C81 present reproducibility analysis results supported by Figure 4F showing variation per effect and variation per model. The statistical comparison (Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA followed by Mann-Whitney tests with Bonferroni correction, p<0.001) demonstrates significant differences. The conclusion about model-to-model variability as the main reproducibility factor is well-supported by the comprehensive analysis across 30 pairwise comparisons.

results.result: Transfer learning from pretrained models reduces training iterations and yields higher validity compared to training from scratch. Frozen pretrained models performed poorly on dissimilar images but matched human expert performance on highly similar datasets, demonstrating the importance of task similarity.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 present transfer learning results supported by data from four external datasets (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1-2) and appropriate citations (Yosinski et al., 2014; Oquab et al., 2014; Bayramoglu and Heikkilä, 2016; Falk et al., 2019). The performance differences between frozen models on similar vs. dissimilar datasets (Lab-Mue vs. Lab-Wue2) provide clear evidence for the role of task similarity. Model selection criteria are clearly defined and applied consistently.

results.result: The consensus ensemble workflow was validated across four external datasets from different laboratories, model organisms (mice and zebrafish), and imaging conditions. All DL approaches detected the expected biological effects confirmed by manual expert analysis, with ensembles showing reduced variation in effect sizes. The workflow is reproducible and increases objectivity, reliability, and validity.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C73 present external validation results supported by data from Lab-Mue, Lab-Inns1, Lab-Inns2, and Lab-Wue2 (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1-2, Table 1). Statistical analyses are appropriate (Mann-Whitney-U tests, some with Bonferroni correction). The biological effects detected by DL approaches match manual expert analyses across diverse experimental conditions. The conclusion about reproducibility across laboratories and datasets is well-supported by the comprehensive external validation.

results.result: Training DL models on single expert annotations incorporates individual human bias and merely automates manual annotation without removing subjective biases. Multiple expert annotations are imperative to mitigate bias and assess model performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 present key conclusions supported by the similarity analysis data (Figure 2) and bioimage analysis results (Figure 4), with appropriate citations (Schmitz et al., 1999; Collier et al., 2003; Niedworok et al., 2016; Falk et al., 2019; von Chamier et al., 2019). The evidence from expert 1 models failing to detect biological effects provides strong support for the bias incorporation claim. The conclusion is a reasonable inference from the comprehensive data analysis.

results.result: Fine-tuned models require fewer training iterations than training from scratch and show reliability at least equivalent to from scratch ensembles. Pretrained ensembles can be used without adaptation if task similarity is sufficiently high, though adapted models typically outperform general models trained on different domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84, C87 present transfer learning findings supported by data from external datasets (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 5) and citations (Falk et al., 2019; Caicedo et al., 2019). The comparison of training iterations, reliability metrics, and performance across initialization variants is well-documented. The conclusion about task similarity is supported by the contrasting performance of frozen models on Lab-Mue vs. Lab-Wue2.

results.result: Sharing validated model weights in open-source libraries could provide annotation experience across laboratories, improve objectivity, and contribute to better reproducibility. The learned representations from cFOS consensus ensembles may serve as good initialization for nucleosomatic fluorescent label segmentation tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86, C88 are primarily speculative about future applications and potential benefits, supported by citations (Falk et al., 2019; Fanelli, 2018) but not directly tested in the study. While the reasoning is sound and the potential benefits are plausible based on the study's findings, these claims represent discussion points about future work rather than demonstrated results. The speculation is reasonable but lacks direct experimental validation.

results.result: The study's focus on U-Net architecture is both a standardization choice and a limitation. Human perception is worse for complex graphical features (area, volume, density) than linear features, and DL models based on human annotations are not suitable for tasks where complete annotation is virtually impossible.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 discuss study limitations and scope, supported by appropriate citations (Ronneberger et al., 2015; Cleveland and McGill, 1985; Feldman-Stewart et al., 2000; Driscoll et al., 2019). The acknowledgment of limitations is appropriate and well-reasoned. The claims about human perceptual limitations and the unsuitability of human-annotation-based DL for complex tasks are supported by cited literature and represent honest assessment of the method's scope.

results.result: Ground truth estimation from multiple human annotators establishes objectivity in fluorescent feature annotations. Ensembles of models trained on estimated ground truth establish reliability and validity. The authors recommend using multiple expert annotations to train and evaluate DL consensus model ensembles to increase objectivity, reliability, and validity of bioimage analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C29-C30, C92-C93 present the study's main conclusions, supported by comprehensive data from similarity analysis (Figure 2), bioimage analysis (Figures 3-4), and external validation (Figure 5). The progression from establishing objectivity through consensus models to achieving reliability and validity through ensembles is well-demonstrated across multiple datasets and laboratories. The recommendations are well-justified by the extensive experimental evidence.

results.result: Low-quality annotations can cause DL algorithms to fail training or reproduce inconsistent annotations. While DL models can hold advantages over conventional algorithms, their flexibility makes them prone to internalizing subjective human biases. Standard performance assessment using similarity measures is insufficient to establish trust in DL models for bioimage analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C74-C76 present discussion points about DL challenges and limitations, supported by appropriate citations (von Chamier et al., 2019; Falk et al., 2019; Caicedo et al., 2019; Ronneberger et al., 2015; McQuin et al., 2018; Haberl et al., 2018). These claims synthesize established knowledge from the field and are consistent with the study's findings about bias incorporation in expert models. The reasoning is sound and well-supported by cited literature.
